The relationships examined in this report helped build aerospace capabilities inside China’s military industrial base that could support PLA modernization. Over the past year, the United States House Select Committee on Strategic Competition between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party (“Select Committee”) investigated Western aerospace ties to the PRC’s military industrial base through company records, public source research, interviews with market participants, and engagement with foreign governments. The Select Committee requested and reviewed information from General Electric (“GE”) Aerospace, Honeywell Aerospace, and Collins Aerospace concerning their PRC operations and relationships with PRC defense entities such as the Aviation Industry Corporation of China (“AVIC”) and the Commercial Aircraft Corporation of China (“COMAC”). On the surface it may seem as though all aerospace companies play by the same rules, but they do not. While American firms are subject to oversight from Congress and the executive branch, France enacted a law that actively obstructs American oversight. At the same time, French aerospace companies sell dual-use products, engage in co-development with Chinese military entities, and further PRC dual-use technologies across several capabilities. In particular, Airbus systemically furthered China’s aerospace industrial base spanning decades. Beginning in 2006, Airbus Helicopters (then Eurocopter) jointly developed the Z- 15 helicopter with the Harbin Aircraft Industry Group (HAIG),F23 while the same company developed military helicopters for the PLA.F24 HAIG’s first engagement with Eurocopter Group started in the early 1980s. In 2023, Airbus announced the sale of helicopters advertised with stealth capabilities to a Chinese state-owned firm.F 25 In October 2025, Airbus announced the opening of the second final assembly line (“FAL”) in Tianjin, China. F26 Airbus also actively encouraged key suppliers to relocate from Europe to China. F27 As a result of Airbus’s support for the Chinese aerospace industry, certain unilateral American sanctions would only provide an opening for Airbus to increase its market share. This report refers to this issue as the “Backfill Problem” where allied aerospace companies can backfill capabilities in the event the United States applied unilateral sanctions on the Chinese aerospace industry. The Select Committee found that the problem was systemic, not confined to any one transaction or company. The broader system allowed commercial aerospace engagement that could strengthen firms connected to the PRC’s military industrial base without triggering the safeguards designed to protect sensitive technology. The Select Committee does not investigate in the first instance to find potential violations of law; it seeks to illuminate areas where policymakers should consider change and generate policy recommendations. The Select Committee therefore makes the following findings: • Finding 1: Western aerospace companies entered lawful commercial arrangements that transferred advanced technology, technical know-how, and Western expertise to Chinese aerospace firms. • Finding 2: Honeywell Aerospace, GE Aerospace, and Collins Aerospace repeatedly sought and obtained licenses for controlled technology transfers involving PRC military end users and other military-linked entities as part of Chinese commercial aerospace platforms. • Finding 3: Export controls relied on company due diligence even where commercial incentives favored continuity and past enforcement actions revealed compliance weaknesses. • Finding 4: PRC-based joint ventures created a structural gap in U.S. national security review by allowing sensitive capabilities to move offshore outside the principal Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (“CFIUS”) framework. • Finding 5: Unilateral U.S. restrictions would disadvantage American aerospace companies without denying China access to many Western technologies when allied firms backfill the resulting business. Based on these findings, the Select Committee makes a series of policy recommendations to address defense contractors working for both the U.S. and Chinese industrial base, strengthening aerospace export controls, and tightening investment restrictions in the aerospace sector. Initially, the Select Committee addresses the issue of allied defense contractors, namely Airbus, benefiting both as a Pentagon contractor while simultaneously investing in the Chinese aerospace industrial base. This practice should be halted, and defense contractors must pick a side. Additionally, the United States must strengthen aerospace export controls on sales to China. However, the United States needs to work with allies and partners to jointly restrict this activity and its associated investment. Unilateral American restrictions may deprive China of certain capabilities, but they will also create an opening for European aerospace firms to backfill. Moreover, the U.S. government must require disclosure of these ties so government procurement officers can make informed decisions about how to award taxpayer funds. Finally, the U.S. should not sell its capabilities to European companies working with Chinese military entities. As discussed below, certain countries, mainly France, have a blocking statute that prohibits them from sharing information with the U.S. government as part of an investigation. Airbus even informed the Select Committee that when they were investigated by the Department of Justice, the blocking statute prohibited the sharing of documents. In this environment, U.S regulators cannot adequately investigate whether export control violations took place, making enforcement nearly impossible. CFIUS must address this situation by subjecting these countries to greater scrutiny when they acquire U.S. companies. These policy recommendations are detailed more fully at the conclusion of this report. These findings are best understood in the context of how the PRC organizes its aerospace industry. The Chinese firms that partnered with Western companies were not isolated commercial enterprises. They operated within a state-directed industrial system that concentrated aviation, propulsion, space, missile, and electronic capabilities across a small number of large conglomerates and their extensive networks of subsidiaries, research institutes, suppliers, and investment vehicles.

blocks.text: During the 1990s and 2000s, Beijing repeatedly reorganized its aviation industry to consolidate major capabilities under large state-owned enterprises. The state domination of the sector signals Beijing’s strategic view of the aerospace sector. In 2008, the PRC recombined its two principal aviation conglomerates to form AVIC, the country’s principal military aviation conglomerate and a major producer of military platforms.F 28 AVIC oversees a sprawling network of thousands of subordinate entities, including subsidiaries, research institutes, factories, laboratories, departments, and workshops. F29 Its scale and breadth are roughly comparable to combining Lockheed Martin, Boeing Defense, Northrop Grumman, and several other major aerospace suppliers under one roof. Through its subsidiaries and research institutes, AVIC designs and manufactures most of the PLA’s domestically produced military aircraft, including the J-20 stealth fighter, J-10 and J-16 fighters, Y-20 strategic transport, H-6 bomber, KJ-500 airborne early warning aircraft, Z-10 attack helicopter, and multiple families of unmanned aircraft.F30 AVIC described MCF as its “historical mission” and “strengthening the military” as a primary responsibility. F31 Unlike its Western counterparts, AVIC’s primary duty is not to shareholders, but to the PRC party-state and its defense goals.F32 In recognition of this role, the U.S. Department of the Treasury designated AVIC as a Non-SDN Chinese Military-Industrial Complex Company (“NS- CMIC”) in 2021.F33 The same year as AVIC’s combination, 2008, Beijing established COMAC to lead development of large commercial aircraft, namely the ARJ21 (later renamed the C909), C919, and C929 commercial aircraft. F34 Although COMAC’s ties to the PRC defense industrial base are less overt than AVIC’s, its own records trace its core design institute directly to the 708 Engineering Design Group, formerly part of PLA Air Force Factory 5703.F 35 Moreover, AVIC’s involvement in COMAC signals COMAC’s military applications. Although AVIC holds a minority share in COMAC, it maintains outsized influence on COMAC’s operations. F 36 Much of COMAC’s original leadership, employees, facilities, and technology came from AVIC, and COMAC continues to draw on AVIC talent and technology. F37 The C919, China’s commercial narrow-body airliner, has been repeatedly linked to the PRC’s military-civil fusion strategy. Chinese military commentators identified it as a potential replacement for Y-8 and Y-9 special mission aircraft, including airborne early warning, reconnaissance, and anti-submarine platforms,F 38 while a study coauthored by a PLA Naval Service Academy researcher called for using it to “develop new military aircraft” and “accelerate the modernization of the Chinese Air Force.” F39 PRC authorities have likewise held up the C919 as a product of the aviation sector’s “deep development of military-civil fusion,”F40 and in 2022, Xi Jinping called the program an embodiment of the “will of the state.”F41 Figure 2. blocks.text: Beijing built similar institutional structures around other critical aerospace capabilities. The Aero Engine Corporation of China (“AECC”) consolidates China’s military and civilian aircraft engine industry. F 44 The China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (“CASC”) and China Aerospace Science and Industry Corporation (“CASIC”) anchor major space and missile programs, while the China Electronics Technology Group Corporation (“CETC”) and China Electronics Corporation (“CEC”) underpin much of the military electronics and information technology base. F45 Together, these conglomerates sit atop extensive networks of subsidiaries, research institutes, laboratories, manufacturers, investment vehicles, and industrial partners. F46 Building the institutions was only part of the challenge. Beijing also had to acquire technologies, know-how, and expertise that its domestic aerospace industry did not possess. It poured state capital, research funding, and industrial resources into indigenous development, while turning outward to fill remaining capability gaps through two principal channels: illicit acquisition and lawful commercial partnerships. Over time, lawful commercial engagement offered a broader pathway. Beijing opened civil aviation to foreign investment and joint ventures then encouraged multinational firms to bring capital, technology, R&D capabilities, and management expertise into strategic high-technology sectors, including aviation. F47 During this time, the United States operated under the naïve assumption that commercial engagement with the PRC would lead to political liberalization. As a result, the United States encouraged companies to set up businesses in the PRC to take advantage of the significant market opportunity and grow their business. By 2017, AVIC established 16 joint ventures with foreign aerospace companies to supply critical systems for the C919, including avionics, flight controls, electrical power, fuel systems, and landing gear. F48 However, this pattern of military-civil fusion long predates the C919. As Figure 3 shows, PRC aerospace programs have used foreign or commercially oriented aircraft and technologies as starting points then iterated and adapted these platforms to meet military needs. Figure 3. Selected Cases of Foreign and Commercial Aerospace Capabilities Carried into PRC Military Programs The cases differ in their details, but the Select Committee’s analysis revealed a similar playbook: foreign aircraft, components, and technical know-how entered China through commercial or other non-military channels, then helped build the engineering expertise, manufacturing capacity, supplier base, and systems- integration capabilities needed for later civilian and military programs. Initial iterations of these platforms were designed for commercial use, while later iterations were adapted for the military. PRC officials described these commercial relationships as vehicles for building precisely those indigenous capabilities. The Ministry of Science and Technology (“MOST”) said the C919 mastered more than 100 core and key technologies and credited international joint ventures with helping develop domestic propulsion, avionics, flight control, power, fuel, and landing gear industries. F 49 The Civil Aviation Administration of China (“CAAC”) made a similar point about the Y-7-200A, later renamed the MA-60, saying AVIC Xi’an Aircraft Industry Group Company Limited (“XAC”) developed the aircraft by “absorbing advanced aviation technology” and “making extensive use of mature foreign components,” including Pratt & Whitney’s PW127C engine. F50 AVIC described development of the Z-8 from the French SA-321 Super Frelon in even more explicit terms, calling it a process of “introduction, digestion, absorption, and re-innovation.”F51 Commercial aerospace partnerships build capabilities that extend far beyond a single aircraft. Transferred hardware, software, and joint-venture expertise allow Chinese engineers to master system integration, factories to refine precision manufacturing, and suppliers to meet aerospace standards. Crucially, state- backed defense firms accumulate the tooling, production data, workforce, and management know-how that carry directly into subsequent platforms. F 52 Civil transfers today directly build the industrial capacity needed for PRC military platforms tomorrow.F53 The national security significance of these partnerships extends beyond the platform named in a license application. Aerospace capability is cumulative and generational: expertise, production capacity, and supplier networks built for one program can persist and support later ones. The C919 sits at the center of that dynamic. The sections below examine how Western joint ventures and technology transfers helped build C919 capabilities that the PRC aerospace sector can localize, absorb, and apply across future programs.

Across their productions to the Select Committee, the aerospace companies consistently portrayed their involvement in the PRC’s defense industrial base as discrete, limited, and lawful. That framing misses the cumulative effect of their activities. Beijing did not need any one Western company to supply an entire aircraft to upgrade its aerospace sector. It needed different companies to fill capability gaps. As shown in the chart above, those contributions spanned avionics, surveillance, flight controls, electrical power, and braking. Each company’s role may have been narrow in isolation, but together those roles helped Beijing assemble many of the technological capabilities needed to build an indigenous aerospace industry.

blocks.text: In 2012, Honeywell China established a joint venture to produce C919 components with Hunan Boyun New Materials Co., Ltd. (“Boyun”). Boyun operates as a PRC defense enterprise built to commercialize Huang Boyun’s aerospace expertise in indigenous aircraft-braking systems after he received his Ph.D. in the United States, F63 and conducted postdoctoral research in Tennessee. F64 The partnership also extended to Boyun’s wholly owned subsidiary, Changsha Xinhang Wheel & Brake Co., Ltd. (“Xinhang”), a PLA defense contractor, through ancillary agreements requiring Honeywell Aerospace to transfer technology and provide technical assistance to Xinhang. F65 Honeywell Aerospace owns 51 percent of HBAS and Boyun 49 percent, with equal board representation. Honeywell Aerospace seconds two employees to the venture, including its general manager. F66 A 2012 Technology License Agreement among Honeywell Aerospace, Boyun, Xinhang, and HBAS governs any access that Boyun or Xinhang may obtain relative to Honeywell Aerospace 's "C919 Background Technology", as well as Honeywell Aerospace's access to Boyun technology.F 67 The Honeywell Aerospace technology conveyed to Boyun was limited to C919 carbon brake disc geometry requirements, while the technology conveyed to Xinhang was specific to the machining of structural parts as defined in the workshare agreement. F68 Under the division of labor, Honeywell Aerospace provided components, machining, and coating technology, Boyun supplied its proprietary Thermal Gradient Chemical Vapor Infiltration (“CVI”) process for carbon discs, and Xinhang conducted dynamometer testing, with HBAS integrating the final assembly.F69 Honeywell Aerospace represented to the Select Committee that the workshare in place today is limited to carbon disc manufacturing, with densification  using Boyun's proprietary CVI process, machining and antioxidant coating protection using Honeywell Aerospace's technology, and Xinhang performing dynamometer testing. The parties, however, defined the venture’s technical scope in contrasting terms. In correspondence with Select Committee staff, Honeywell Aerospace maintained that HBAS focuses on “safety assurance, not technical advancement” and “does not engage in design, engineering, or R&D activities.”F70 Boyun, by contrast, informed its investors that HBAS would execute full wheel-and-brake system “design, research and development, testing, component manufacturing, [and] system assembly.” F71 The limits of Boyun’s technical contribution became evident when its carbon braking material failed to meet performance variation and durability requirements necessary to support aircraft certification..F 72 Although Honeywell Aerospace worked with COMAC to find a path to certify Boyun's baseline CVI process for the C919, Boyun used the qualification failure to request an export license for Honeywell Aerospace’s proprietary Isothermal Chemical Vapor Infiltration (“ICVI”) process, an advanced method needed to produce ultra-durable carbon brakes.F 73 Honeywell Aerospace refused the request and kept the technology outside China. The episode nevertheless demonstrated how a commercial partnership could be used by a PRC defense contractor to upgrade its domestic baseline and seek restricted U.S. technology when local capabilities fell short. Beyond individual technology transfers, the C919 program provided the physical foundation to expand PRC military production. Boyun's corporate filings confirm that while Honeywell Aerospace's technical assistance targeted civilian C919 manufacturing, Boyun used the broader expansion driven by the C919 program to enlarge physical facilities and testing equipment that were engineered to concurrently supply C919 components and domestic "military fighters and transport aircraft."F74 The physical footprint reflected the same commercial-military overlap. HBAS, Boyun, and Xinhang are clustered in Changsha’s Lugu industrial base, as shown in Figure 4. A 2014 article by a department director at the National University of Defense Technology (“NUDT”) F 75 identified the introduction of Honeywell to jointly produce large-aircraft wheel-and-brake systems as an example of the region’s “deepening” military-civil cooperation. F 76 By 2016, Hunan authorities described Lugu as home to more than 100 enterprises engaged in MCF, specifically identifying Boyun and HoneywellF77 within its large-aircraft industrial cluster, and described NUDT as an important source of technical expertise for the local MCF industry.F78 Figure 4. Co-Location of HBAS, Boyun, and Xinhang in Changsha Against that backdrop, Boyun and Xinhang continued to expand their aerospace capabilities. Boyun’s government subsidies rose from roughly 3 million RMB (approximately $447,000) in 2011 to approximately 12 million RMB (approximately $1.7M) in 2012 as the Honeywell Aerospace joint venture and C919 program were getting underway.F79 By November 2014, the new production facility was operating two months ahead of schedule, and by 2016, Xinhang was mass- producing wheel-and-brake systems for existing military aircraft platforms.F80 The C919 wheel-and-brake system Xinhang was developing with Honeywell Aerospace was a distinct product line that had not yet entered mass production. Xinhang’s patent activity also increased during the Honeywell Aerospace relationship, as shown in Figure 5. Figure 5. Xinhang Patent Activity While patent activity alone does not prove technology transfer, the increase is consistent with Boyun and Xinhang’s own statements that they were expanding their aerospace capabilities during the Honeywell Aerospace relationship.F 81 Overall, these developments contributed to the same ecosystem. By 2020, local reporting described the lab that created the C919 brake technologies as also supplying copper-carbon sealing rings for Long March 5, 6, and 7 rockets. F 82 However, the Select Committee did not identify any evidence showing the learnings from the joint venture were applied to the Long March.

blocks.text: In 2013, Honeywell China and AVIC Xi'an Flight Automatic Control Research Institute ("FACRI") established HonFei Flight Controls Technology Co., Ltd. ("HonFei") in Xi'an to design, develop, produce, test, qualify, sell and market C919 flight-control systems.F83 FACRI, also known as AVIC’s 618 Institute, develops civilian and military flight-control technologies, including systems for the PLA’s J-10, J-11, J-15, and J-16 fighter aircraft.F84 The U.S. government designated FACRI a military end user and subjected it to export-control restrictions in 2020.F85 Honeywell China and FACRI each own 50 percent of HonFei, with equal representation on its eight-member board.F86 Day-to-day operations are led by a Honeywell Aerospace-seconded general manager and a FACRI-nominated deputy general manager.F87 Honeywell Aerospace secondsF88 three employees to the venture, including the general manager. F 89 Honeywell Aerospace’s joint venture records identify FACRI official Song Kepu as a signatory to the agreement establishing HonFei.F 90 Song, who later served as FACRI director and HonFei chairman, previously worked on flight-control systems for the JH-7 fighter jet, JF- 17 fighter jet, and an unnamed missile-guidance system.F91 Honeywell Aerospace described HonFei’s operational role as “primarily logistical” and said the venture did not conduct “final testing, assembly, or new product engineering.”F92 The governing agreements, however, assigned HonFei a broader technical role. Under the 2013 “C919 FCS Cooperative Technology Development Contract,” Honeywell Aerospace, FACRI, and HonFei were assigned development work and HonFei received a royalty-free license under Honeywell Aerospace’s “Sole Foreground Technology” to “design, develop, test, qualify, make, have made, sell, offer to sell, import and export” the flight-control system or its components.F 93 A separate Flight Control Technology License Agreement entitled FACRI and HonFei to receive “data, know-how, and assistance” needed for their development workshares, even as Honeywell Aerospace retained tight control over its source code. F 94 Taken together, these agreements show that HonFei was structured to perform technical development functions beyond the logistical role Honeywell Aerospace emphasized in its correspondence with Select Committee staff. Honeywell Aerospace’s own description of the HonFei facility, together with public reporting and satellite imagery analyzed by the Select Committee, indicates a broader operational and technical role than logistics alone. The imagery shows HonFei physically co-located within FACRI’s broader footprint in the Xi’an High- Tech Industries Development Zone, as shown in Figure 6. That location is itself significant. By 2015, PRC state media reported that eight of the PRC’s eleven major defense conglomerates had established operations in the zone across aviation, aerospace, military electronics, weapons, shipbuilding, and nuclear industries, and explicitly cited Honeywell’s partnership with FACRI as an example of MCF activity there.F95 Figure 6. Co-Location of HonFei and FACRI in the Xi’an High-Tech Industries Development Zone Honeywell Aerospace’s representations to the Select Committee further indicate that the site contained production, repair, and quality-control functions subject to physical and information controls restricting FACRI personnel from sensitive areas and technical data. F96 The arrangement therefore placed meaningful aerospace production and technical capabilities alongside FACRI personnel and relied on Honeywell Aerospace’s internal controls to keep sensitive functions segregated. Honeywell Aerospace represented that those controls were effective, but the Select Committee was unable to independently verify those boundaries since they were physically located in China.F97 This established foundation soon bore fruit outside the C919 program. Honeywell Aerospace later confirmed that HonFei employees developed a drone- related package-delivery mechanism that the venture patented in the PRC and treated as “Joint Venture IP.” F98 Honeywell Aerospace and HonFei have since quarantined all drone related hardware and technology and Honeywell Aerospace is no longer engaged in any drone-related work in China. Around the same period, FACRI was also filing patents covering onboard database and resource-management software,F 99 online software loading,F 100 and AI-enabled scene-matching navigation.F101 Taken as a whole, the Honeywell Aerospace case illustrates China’s pattern for aerospace development. First, create a “commercial” program to lure in a Western aerospace firm into investing in the Chinese aerospace industrial base. Second, work with that aerospace firm to level up the Chinese company’s capabilities and independent technical developments. Third, apply the technology to programs of strategic importance.

GE Aerospace’s importance to U.S. national security extends across generations of military aircraft, with its engines powering platforms including the B-2 bomber; F-15 and F-16 fighters; and Black Hawk and Apache helicopters. F105 That role makes GE Aerospace’s extensive presence in the PRC aerospace sector particularly consequential, given documented failures to prevent sensitive U.S. aerospace technology from reaching the PRC.106 F GE Aerospace’s footprint dates to 1980 and has since expanded across engine sales, maintenance, manufacturing, training, and technical support, with more than 7,800 engines in service and its only 24-hour fleet support center outside the United States located in Shanghai.F107 GE Aerospace characterizes this business as primarily focused on servicing customer engines and says its sole PRC manufacturing site produces only “low-complexity, conventional engine hardware.” F108 Contemporaneous GE Aerospace press releases discuss production of low pressure turbine disks, engine seals, high pressure turbine shafts, compressor shafts, and high pressure turbine blade retainers.F109  Within that broader footprint, however, GE Aerospace also became a key Western partner in the PRC’s commercial aircraft programs, including the C919.

blocks.text: In January 2011, GE Aerospace and AVIC Civil Aviation Electronics Co., Ltd. (“AVIC CAE”) established Aviage Systems Co., Ltd. (“Aviage”) in Shanghai to supply avionics systems for COMAC aircraft, including the C919. F110 AVIC CAE is a subsidiary of AVIC, the state-owned defense conglomerate that develops military aircraft for the PLA, and serves as a corporate bridge to AVIC’s defense avionics enterprise.F111 As part of the deal, GE transferred foundational intellectual property for integrated modular avionics (“IMA”) for use on COMAC aircraft. IMA represents a core dual-use architecture that serves as the digital processing backbone for both commercial airliners and advanced PLA fighters like the J-20.F112 GE Aerospace and AVIC CAE each own 50 percent of Aviage, with representation split across its board and executive leadership.F113 GE Aerospace contributed baseline IMA intellectual property in a “one and done” transfer, while AVIC provided roughly $650 million to fund development. F114 Aviage employed about 300 people, with 85 percent being engineers, who used that baseline technology to build a C919-specific branch as COMAC’s requirements evolved.F115 Provisions in a later contract amendment show military diversion risks were expressly anticipated, establishing a two-year post-employment ban on joining PLA-oriented enterprises, granting GE audit rights, and requiring periodic civil- only compliance reports. The Select Committee, however, cannot independently verify Aviage’s governance or partner obligations because GE Aerospace withheld the underlying joint venture agreement despite repeated staff requests and two direct requests from Chairman Moolenaar in late 2025 and May 2026. Although GE allowed staff to review the agreement’s first amendment, withholding the original and complete document prevents the Committee from assessing Aviage’s initial scope, partner responsibilities, or claims that the deal had been “carefully negotiated” to protect GE Aerospace’s intellectual property. F116 GE Aerospace nevertheless portrayed Aviage to the Select Committee as a narrowly scoped civil venture. The company stated that Aviage was formed with a “civil-only subsidiary of AVIC,” that its activities were “primarily supporting the C919 aircraft,” and that GE remained the “sole developer” of exported U.S. technology while partner entities were excluded from product development. F117 Publicly available information and government records show GE Aerospace’s joint venture partner worked hand-in-hand with AVIC’s military enterprises. GE Aerospace produced two Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (“BIS”) licenses detailing exports to China. They show that as late as 2023, GE Aerospace was actively exporting, with U.S. government approval, controlled C919 avionics hardware, software, and technology to Aviage for development, certification testing, production, and use, after which Aviage integrated those inputs directly into the aircraft’s broader avionics architecture. F118 AVIC CAE was not meaningfully separate from AVIC’s military avionics enterprise. Corporate records show that AVIC CAE is 45 percent owned by AVIC Aerospace Systems Co., Ltd., which is itself 94.91 percent owned directly by AVIC.F 119 Because AVIC Aerospace Systems oversees AVIC’s primary military avionics portfolio, AVIC CAE is directly controlled through AVIC’s defense apparatus. This ownership had a real-world impact on the company’s operations. In one instance, Aviage subcontracted specific components, including the cockpit display system, to AVIC Aeronautical Radio Electronics Research Institute (“615 Institute”), a major AVIC military research institute that develops systems for both civilian and military aircraft, including the J-8, J-10, and J-20 fighter jets.F120 The two entities also shared senior personnel, including Li Feng, who held leadership roles at AVIC CAE and the 615 Institute, while former 615 Institute director Wang Guoqing later became Aviage’s Chief Aircraft Systems Engineer.F121 When the C919 program encountered difficulties in 2020, the institute reassigned personnel from its military aircraft programs to the effort and formed a joint team with COMAC and Aviage that met daily to work through development tasks.F122 As Figure 7 shows, the 615 Institute sits across the street from Aviage in Shanghai’s Zizhu High-Tech Industrial Development Zone. Figure 7. Map of Zizhu High-Tech Industrial Development Zone Moreover, Aviage’s activities were not limited to, or even framed by its own leadership, as principally about the C919. In a 2021 interview, Aviage President Zhang Yuanzhong said the company was established “not for the C919 project alone,” but to “jointly develop the new field of civil avionics.” F123  He said Aviage had since expanded into cockpit speech recognition, AI analysis of flight data, airborne BeiDou communications and navigation, and the C929 widebody program.F124  Zhang also said that while “many resources” initially came from GE Aerospace, Aviage’s personnel and engineering capabilities, particularly in system integration, had grown beyond GE Aerospace’s own business scope.

blocks.text: Collins Aerospace, a business of RTX Corporation (“RTX”), is one of the world’s largest aerospace and defense systems suppliers. It was formed in November 2018, when United Technologies Corporation (“UTC”) acquired Rockwell Collins, Inc. (“Rockwell Collins”) and combined it with UTC Aerospace Systems. In April 2020, UTC merged with Raytheon Company to form Raytheon Technologies Corporation, renamed RTX Corporation in 2023. Collins Aerospace remains a principal RTX business, supplying avionics, communications, navigation, sensors, flight controls, and other systems used across commercial as well as U.S. and allied military aircraft. Against that backdrop, Collins Aerospace’s extensive ties to the PRC aerospace sector are particularly consequential. Through Collins Aerospace and its predecessor companies, the company established at least three joint ventures with PRC aerospace and defense entities supporting the C919 program, including surveillance, communications and navigation, and aircraft electrical power systems. These ventures were part of a broader PRC footprint that included ten operating sites and eight joint ventures. As discussed in the following section, Collins Aerospace also identified multiple MEU licenses across its AVIC joint ventures.F130 Those relationships persisted even as Beijing retaliated against Collins Aerospace’s parent company for supporting U.S. security commitments to Taiwan. In October 2020, Beijing announced sanctions against Raytheon over U.S. arms sales to Taiwan, and in February 2022 announced unspecified countermeasures on Raytheon Technologies Corporation under the PRC’s Anti- Foreign Sanctions Law.F131

blocks.text: In 2012, Rockwell Collins established AVIC Leihua Rockwell Collins Avionics Co., Ltd. (“ALRAC”) with Wuxi AVIC Leihua Avionics Equipment Co., Ltd. (“AVIC Wuxi”) to develop and produce integrated surveillance systems (“ISS”) for the C919.F132 AVIC Wuxi was later deregistered, and current corporate records identify AVIC Wuxi Radar Technology Co., Ltd. (“AVIC Wuxi Radar”) as ALRAC’s AVIC shareholder. F133 Documents produced to the Select Committee show that Suzhou Changfeng Aviation Electronics Co., Ltd. (“Suzhou Changfeng”), then operating as AVIC (Suzhou) Radar and Electronic Technology Co., Ltd. (“AVIC Suzhou Radar”), and AVIC Leihua Electronic Technology Research Institute (“LETRI”) were also parties to related agreements governing the venture, including a separate Work Allocation Agreement assigning LETRI a technical role in the C919 surveillance system. F134 The Select Committee’s review of the underlying agreements shows a stark mismatch between capital contributions and economic returns. Under the 2012 agreement, AVIC Wuxi contributed 99 percent of ALRAC’s registered capital and Rockwell Collins just 1 percent, while the parties split profits equally. F135 Rockwell Collins primarily contributed intellectual property. That structure suggests the parties placed substantial value on the intellectual property Rockwell Collins brought to the venture. The agreement also spells out what Rockwell Collins was expected to bring to the venture and what the Chinese side was meant to gain from it. Rockwell Collins would contribute its “advanced avionics technology” and “international avionics technical services,” while ALRAC would use those capabilities to build Chinese “self-innovation capability” and “boost the development and prosperity of the commercial aviation sector of the PRC.” F136 Those transfers remained subject to U.S. export controls, and Collins Aerospace obtained licenses to continue ISS-related work after BIS designated LETRI as a Military End User (“MEU”) in 2020.F137 The parties further committed to making ALRAC a “center of excellence in the PRC” for the surveillance system and other avionics products, F138 a broader objective not expressly limited to civilian applications. F139 The significance of that capability-building effort becomes clearer when viewed against the identities of ALRAC’s Chinese participants. AVIC Wuxi Radar is wholly owned by AVIC Airborne Systems Co., Ltd. (“AVIC Airborne Systems”), AVIC’s principal platform for military avionics and airborne electromechanical systems.F140 LETRI, also known as the 607 Institute, is AVIC’s principal airborne radar research institute and has long developed radar systems for Chinese combat aircraft, including the JL-7 and JL-10A.F141 Suzhou Changfeng is an AVIC avionics research and development unit whose work includes integrated displays, aircraft intake controls, and engine measurement and control systems for military aircraftF142 and Unmanned Aerial Vehicles.F143 Furthermore, as shown in Figure 8, ALRAC is located in the Wuxi National Integrated Circuit Design Center, a roughly 50-acre government-backed research and development park housing more than 160 integrated-circuit and related companies.F144 Tenants include CETC subsidiaries China Key System & Integrated Circuit Co., Ltd. (“CKSIC”) and Wuxi Microelectronics Research Center (“CETC’s 58th Research Institute”).F145 Chinese sources identify CKSIC as a core military integrated-circuit research and production institute and a major supplier of military chips,F 146 while CETC’s 58th Research Institute is described as a “key backbone” for the “research, development, and production of military integrated circuits.”F 147 The institute also jointly operates a key laboratory with Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics F148  focused on chips and microsystems for “aviation, aerospace, and national defense,”F149 which has separately worked with COMAC on large-aircraft component validation, airworthiness research, technical standards, and related technology development. F150 Collins Aerospace represented to the Select Committee that ALRAC does not work with these parties and has not provided any information to them, as reflected in Collins Aerospace’s licenses. F 151 Since these facilities are physically located in China, the Select Committee was unable to independently verify this statement. Figure 8. ALRAC at the Wuxi National Integrated Circuit Design Center The capability-building envisioned in the 2012 agreements was followed by measurable technical gains. In 2022, two years after being added to the BIS MEU list, LETRI announced a regulatory milestone for a weather-radar flat plate antenna developed by LETRI to meet Collins Aerospace specifications and requirements.F152 This weather-radar antenna received Technical Standard Order (“TSO”) authorization from the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (“FAA”) for COMAC’s C919.F153 At the time of its announcement, one observer highlighted it was the “the first FAA TSO certified avionics component to be developed and manufactured by a company in China, with more on the way.”F154 By 2025, LETRI was advertising a broader portfolio of radar technologies, F155 including advanced weather radar and synthetic aperture radar. F156 Its technical output also increased markedly after ALRAC’s establishment. blocks.text: In 2010, COMAC selected CETC Avionics Co., Ltd. (“CETCA”) and Rockwell Collins to jointly supply the C919’s communications and navigation system through a 50/50, $100 million joint venture in Chengdu. F157 The partners formally established Rockwell Collins CETC Avionics Co., Ltd. (“RCCAC”) in 2014 to develop and assemble the system. From the outset, however, RCCAC was intended to support a broader range of PRC aircraft. At its opening, then Rockwell Collins CEO and President Kelly Ortberg said RCCAC would also support “other programs in China.” F158 That broader mandate placed Collins Aerospace technology inside an enterprise closely tied to the PRC defense industrial base. CETC created CETCA in Chengdu in 2009 by drawing on seven CETC research institutes, several of which developed radar, navigation, communications, command and control, electronic warfare, and computing systems for the PLA. F159 CETCA later described its own business as spanning both “civil aviation and military-civil fusion.” F160 Rockwell Collins technology also was not new to the PRC military aviation sector: its systems were already used aboard PRC military aircraft, including the Y-8 transport.F161 Here again, the Select Committee’s review of the underlying agreements shows a stark mismatch between capital contributions and economic returns. Under the 2014 agreement, CETCA contributed 99 percent of RCCAC’s registered capital and Rockwell Collins just 1 percent, while the parties split profits equally. F162 That structure suggests the parties placed substantial value on what Rockwell Collins brought to the venture beyond cash. The agreement also spells out what Rockwell Collins was expected to bring to the venture and what the Chinese side was meant to gain from it. Rockwell Collins agreed to grant the JV a license to use its “advanced technologies and know-how” for the “purpose of design, development, manufacture, integration, assembly, service/MRO and/or the sale of avionics systems.” F163 The agreement shows the key enabling technology included a significant number of documents detailing how Rockwell Collins managed quality, production output, and testing of key aerospace systems.F164 Those transfers remained subject to U.S. export controls, and Collins Aerospace obtained licenses to continue avionics-related work with CETCA and the joint venture. F165 At some point, the parties were worried that CETCA may be listed under United States export control regulations because they executed an amendment to specifically address that situation. In December 2023, Rockwell Collins executed an amendment to the joint venture that included specifically identifying “the occurrence of … any sanction related restrictions imposed on Rockwell [Collins] or CETCA.”F166 The amendment laid out a process for unwinding the joint venture in the event sanctions were imposed. PRC authorities separately made clear that the partnership was expected to build indigenous capability. The PRC State Administration of Science, Technology and Industry for National Defense (“SASTIND”) said RCCAC would introduce communications and navigation technology comparable to that used on the Boeing 787 and Airbus A350 and enable a “leapfrog improvement” in related PRC technologies.F167  CETCA later credited RCCAC with filling a domestic capability gap and establishing indigenous production and maintenance capacity. RCCAC operated at CETCA’s avionics industrial base at No. 9 Baichuan Road in Chengdu, the same campus as CETC Special Mission Aircraft System Engineering Co., Ltd. (“CETC Special Aircraft”), a developer of unmanned and special mission aircraft formally included in Sichuan’s “military industry system.”F 171 The industrial park sits immediately adjacent to the Huangtianba aviation complex, home to AVIC Chengdu Aircraft Industry Group and the Chengdu Aircraft Design and Research Institute, major centers for PRC fighter and unmanned aircraft development.F172 Collins Aerospace represented to the Select Committee that RCCAC does not work with these parties and has not provided—or contemplated providing—any information to them, as reflected in Collins Aerospace’s licenses. F 173 Since these facilities are physically located in China, the Select Committee was unable to independently verify this statement. Senior personnel likewise crossed between the commercial avionics venture and CETC’s defense businesses. CETCA’s founding chairman, Zuo Qunsheng, had earlier participated in the development and flight testing of China’s first indigenous airborne pulse Doppler fire control radar. F174 Chen Guohai later held senior leadership roles across CETCA and affiliated ventures, including RCCAC, CETC’s now-shuttered joint venture with Thales, and CETC Special Aircraft. Ren Jingsong similarly served as chairman of RCCAC before becoming chairman and general manager of CETC Special Aircraft. These personnel ties further connected the commercial C919 venture to CETC’s military aviation businesses. In May 2021, CETCA increased its stake in RCCAC from 50 percent to 99 percent, effectively taking control while Collins Aerospace retained a 1 percent interest.F175 Collins Aerospace’s ownership of its C919 surveillance joint venture with AVIC Leihua was similarly reduced to 1 percent. The following year, Beijing announced unspecified countermeasures against Collins Aerospace’s parent Raytheon Technologies over its involvement in U.S. arms sales to Taiwan. CETCA subsequently expanded its domestic development and testing capabilities in satellite communications, RNP navigation, and multi-band RCP communications, including platforms for high-reliability equipment designed for complex operating environments. F176 Taken together, the partnership did more than supply a communications and navigation system for a commercial airliner. It helped localize advanced avionics technology, production, and maintenance capabilities inside a CETC enterprise whose facilities, personnel, and institutional structure were closely intertwined with the PRC military aviation sector.

blocks.text: The case studies above show how Western aerospace partnerships helped place technology, engineering expertise, and production capabilities inside the PRC aerospace industrial base. The next question is why U.S. national security safeguards did not prevent those relationships from forming or, once risks became clearer, bring them to an end. In many cases, the answer lies in the commercial framing of the underlying aircraft programs. The partnerships examined by the Select Committee were generally established to support ostensibly civil platforms such as the C919. That framing allowed U.S. companies to continue supplying controlled aerospace hardware, software, technical data, and engineering support under export licenses, even where the Chinese counterparties were closely tied to the PRC defense industrial base. Over time, several of those counterparties were formally identified by the U.S. government as Military End Users, but that designation did not necessarily terminate the commercial relationship. Finding 2: Honeywell Aerospace, GE Aerospace, and Collins Aerospace repeatedly sought and obtained licenses for controlled C919 and ARJ21 transfers involving PRC military end users and other military-linked entities. As part of its investigation, the Select Committee reviewed export licenses produced by GE Aerospace, Honeywell Aerospace, and Collins Aerospace. Those records show how BIS authorized controlled aerospace hardware, software, and technology exports to PRC commercial aircraft programs even where military- linked entities were parties to the transaction. They also show how the licensing process allowed the commercial character of the C919 and ARJ21 programs to remain relevant to BIS’s review despite those military ties. In 2020, BIS acknowledged that the PRC’s Military-Civil Fusion strategy made the distinction between civilian and military development increasingly difficult to maintain and expanded its MEU controls in response. F178 Yet those controls did not categorically bar covered transfers involving military end users. Instead, such transactions could still proceed through the licensing process, where the stated civil end use remained relevant to BIS’s decision. F179 As Figure 10 shows, Honeywell Aerospace, GE Aerospace, and Collins Aerospace first had to determine whether the hardware, software, or technology sought for export was subject to the Export Administration Regulations (“EAR”) and, if so, how it was classified on the Commerce Control List (“CCL”) or designated EAR99. Each listed item may be assigned an Export Control Classification Number (“ECCN”), which identifies the item and the reasons for control. Most of the ECCNs in the licenses produced to the Select Committee fell within Categories 7 and 9, which cover navigation and avionics, and aerospace and propulsion, respectively. Figure 10. Summarized Export Licensing Process for Controlled Transfers F180 Next, the companies had to determine whether any end-use or end-user restrictions applied. General Prohibition Five was most relevant,F 181 because it incorporates several separate restrictions in Part 744, including the Entity List and the military end-use and military end-user rule.F182 The two operate differently. For an Entity List party, the applicable license requirement is set by that entity’s specific listing, which may cover all items subject to the EAR or a narrower set. F183 In contrast, the military end-use and military end-user rule applies only to covered items when the company knows they are destined for a prohibited military end use or military end user.F184 MEU List identifies certain such parties, but “is not […] exhaustive,” so exporters “must conduct their own due diligence” to determine whether unlisted parties also qualify. F 185 For example, a party may appear on DoW’s 1260H Chinese Military Companies list but is absent from the MEU List.

blocks.text: However, this would still raise a “Red Flag” requiring “additional due diligence.”F187 Several PRC parties named in the licenses, including the Shanghai Aircraft Design and Research Institute, FACRI, and LETRI, implicated one or both controls. Multiple transactions involved a covered item and a prohibited military end use or military end user. Once a transaction required a license, the company had to tell BIS what it wanted to export, who would receive or use it, for what purpose, the item’s intended destination, the item’s proposed route, and the potential other counterparties to the transactions.F 188 The Select Committee reviewed granted licenses produced by Honeywell Aerospace, GE Aerospace, and Collins Aerospace. Most involved the C919 or ARJ21, while Collins Aerospace licenses involved other AVIC programs. Taken together, the licenses reveal two broader features of how the expanded controls operated in practice. First, the new military-end-user restrictions often converted existing commercial aerospace work into licensed activity rather than bringing that work to an end. Honeywell Aerospace and Collins Aerospace both described activities that predated the expanded controls and then sought licenses to continue those same activities once the new restrictions applied. The technical work and commercial relationships largely remained in place, while the transfers now required BIS approval and were expressly tied to the C919 or ARJ21 as the authorized civil end use. The controls changed the licensing status of the work more than the work itself. As Figure 11 shows, the resulting licenses continued to authorize controlled avionics, flight-control systems, software, and data transfers in support of those same commercial aircraft programs. Figure 11. License Descriptions Tying Controlled Exports to the C919 and ARJ21 Second, as required by BIS, parties were identified according to their role in the transaction, not necessarily according to the ownership structure behind them. Restrictions generally followed the named entity, not its ownership interests, so a separately incorporated joint venture did not automatically inherit the restrictions of a listed shareholder. A joint venture could therefore be named as the purchaser, consignee, or end user without its PRC shareholder being separately identified. For example, one of Honeywell Aerospace’s license applications identified HonFei as a non-military end user but did not separately identify FACRI, its 50- percent AVIC shareholder and a military end user, as a party to the transaction. F189 By contrast, another license named both HonFei and FACRI in a separate C919 transaction despite the same underlying 50-50 ownership structure.F190 Similarly, both GE Aerospace licenses identified Aviage as the purchaser without separately identifying AVIC CAE, which held 50 percent of Aviage. F191 BIS later moved to close this ownership gap through its September 2025 “Affiliates Rule,” which extended Entity List and Military End-User List restrictions to entities at least 50 percent owned by listed parties. F192 However, the rule was suspended two months later for one year as part of the broader U.S.- China trade negotiations then underway. F193 Once the applicant identified the items, parties, and end use, BIS reviewed the application and decided whether to refer it for interagency review. The EAR directs BIS, “[t]o the maximum extent possible,” to decide license applications “without referral […] to other agencies,” although BIS may seek review from the Departments of War, State, Energy, or other agencies. F194 Generally, BIS would make the final licensing decision under the review policies applicable to each transaction. F195 For China, transactions subject to the military end-use and MEU rule were generally reviewed with a presumption of denial.F 196 For national-security-controlled items exported to the PRC, BIS separately reviewed the risk of diversion to MEUs or military end uses while maintaining a “general policy of approval” for items determined to be for “civil end users [or] for civil end uses.” F197 The companies’ commercial characterization of the transactions was directly relevant to the licensing analysis. By identifying the C919 or ARJ21 as the stated end use, they presented transfers involving military-linked PRC parties as support for civil aircraft programs. While BIS still considered “the appropriateness of the export […] for the stated end use,” the parties involved, and diversion risks, records produced to the Select Committee show that BIS approved numerous C919 and ARJ21 licenses involving military- linked PRC parties.F198 By the time many of these restrictions applied, however, the underlying relationships and technical work had already been in place for years. Joint ventures had been formed, engineering teams worked together, production arrangements had been established, and PRC partners had accumulated experience with major aircraft systems. Subsequent controls could restrict additional transfers, but they could not unwind capabilities, relationships, or infrastructure already created. The purpose of the expanded MEU controls was to prevent U.S. technology from supporting the military capabilities of strategic competitors. In practice, however, the Select Committee assesses that new restrictions often changed the regulatory terms of existing commercial relationships without materially reducing their contributions to PRC military modernization and dual-use aerospace capabilities. Finding 3: Export controls relied on company due diligence even where commercial incentives favored continuity and past enforcement actions revealed compliance weaknesses. The process described above depended heavily on the companies themselves to identify the technology, parties, ownership relationships, and end uses relevant to each transaction. That reliance was not neutral. Honeywell Aerospace, GE Aerospace, and Collins Aerospace had substantial commercial interests in preserving long-standing PRC aerospace relationships, including joint ventures and supplier arrangements tied to the C919 and ARJ21. When new military-end- user restrictions were applied, the records reviewed by the Select Committee suggest that the companies sought licenses to continue those relationships rather than withdraw from them. Regulations gave significant deference to the companies’ own compliance judgments. The licensing process relied on them to classify controlled technology correctly, determine when a license was required, identify military-linked recipients, and prevent unauthorized transfers, even when a more restrictive judgment could limit their own business. Each of the three aerospace companies examined here has faced significant export-control enforcement actions involving failures in those same areas. • In 2021, Honeywell International Inc. agreed to pay $13 million to resolve alleged International Traffic in Arms Regulations

F200 • In 2024, RTX agreed to pay $200 million to resolve 750 alleged ITAR violations. State attributed many of the most serious violations to longstanding compliance weaknesses at Rockwell Collins, including errors in determining the jurisdiction and classification of aerospace technical data and unauthorized releases to PRC recipients. The violations included technical data associated with the E-3, KC-390, and F-22, as well as years of unauthorized exports to PRC suppliers supporting military systems. F201 • In 2026, GE Aerospace agreed to resolve 116 alleged ITAR violations. State Department charging documents described three cases of unauthorized controlled technical data exports to the PRC related to military aircraft engines for multiple DoW platforms, including the F/A-18, U-2, F-16, and F-15 aircraft. The Department attributed the violations to deficiencies in GE’s export-compliance procedures and employees’ failure to follow them. F202 The Select Committee does not cite these enforcement actions to suggest that the C919 or ARJ21 applications reviewed here were inaccurate or improperly obtained. Rather, they illustrate a broader structural concern. The licensing system relies heavily on exporters to identify and elevate national security risks in transactions they have strong commercial incentives to preserve, while offering comparatively little incentive to interpret uncertainty against their own business interests. As Finding 2 shows, those judgments can shape whether an unlisted PRC party is treated as a military end user, whether a joint-venture shareholder is separately identified, and whether longstanding technical work continues under a new license. What this history of significant ITAR violations does show is that the companies’ controls are not always sound. Finding 4: PRC-based joint ventures created a structural gap in U.S. national security review by allowing sensitive capabilities to move offshore outside the principal CFIUS framework. These joint ventures represent a dangerous loophole for draining American technical know-how and diverting it to Chinese firms. As detailed above, many of these joint ventures involved a Western firm transferring its intellectual property and industrial capabilities while the Chinese partner would contribute cash, connections, and labor. Through this relationship, the Chinese joint venture partner is taught how to design, develop, and manufacture technology it would otherwise be unable to learn to produce due to restraints imposed on inbound investment activity by CFIUS. CFIUS would almost certainly block a Chinese state-owned firm from investing or accessing the key intellectual property of U.S. aerospace firms through mergers and acquisitions or other direct investment into the U.S. corporation. But many PRC-based joint ventures circumvent this critical national security review, evading CFIUS jurisdiction and enabling China to lure in Western aerospace companies and bulk up its aerospace industrial base free from unwanted scrutiny by U.S. regulators.

blocks.text: U.S. restrictions do not operate in a vacuum. In a global aerospace market with multiple capable Western suppliers, excluding an American company from the PRC may simply redirect business to an allied competitor rather than deny Beijing the underlying technology or expertise. The result can be a policy that imposes real costs on the U.S. aerospace industrial base while leaving the PRC’s access to Western capabilities largely intact. Finding 5: Unilateral U.S. restrictions would disadvantage American aerospace companies without denying China access to many Western technologies when allied firms backfill the resulting business. Aerospace companies across allied and partner nations compete in many of the same product categories as U.S. firms but operate under different export control, investment, and national security regimes. The C919 program illustrates the problem. COMAC relied not only on American suppliers, but also on European firms for critical systems and components, including propulsion, landing gear, electrical systems, and other aircraft technologies. Where allied rules diverge, U.S. restrictions can therefore shift commercial opportunities away from American firms without producing a corresponding reduction in Beijing’s access to advanced aerospace capabilities. One country plays an outsized role in advancing the PRC’s dual-use aerospace capabilities: France. French aerospace companies have maintained extensive relationships with the PRC aerospace sector for nearly four decades, including with major defense enterprises across aircraft manufacturing, propulsion, software, and other critical technologies. In August 2025, the Select Committee sought to examine those ties more closely, writing to Airbus regarding evidence that its activities in the PRC supported Beijing’s military aerospace capabilities (attached as Attachment A). Airbus subsequently informed the Select Committee that a French blocking law restricted its ability to provide certain information responsive to congressional oversight. This bears emphasis: French law effectively limited the Select Committee’s ability to obtain information from Airbus, a Pentagon contractor, regarding its activities in the PRC. After French authorities constrained Airbus’s engagement, the Committee did not seek comparable productions from Safran or Dassault Systèmes International (“Dassault”) and instead assessed the broader French aerospace sector through open-source research and interviews with market participants. WZ-16 Engines Ongoing During the investigation, multiple market participants told the committee French companies advertise themselves to customers as being beyond the reach of U.S. restrictions. For example, Airbus advertises that it can sell satellite photos without U.S. restrictions. Similarly, Dassault advertises that it can sell to companies identified by the U.S. on the BIS Entity List because it is beyond the reach of U.S. law. The information below corroborates this account because it shows these companies building commercial relationships with entities identified as a national security threat by the United States government. The conclusion of this review is simple: French companies often offer comparable capabilities as American firms, but with far fewer scruples. While American firms have begun taking initial steps to reduce dangerous overexposure to the Chinese market, French firms doubled down on their relationships with PRC firms, especially AVIC. Airbus leads these firms in terms of PRC engagement, but others have strengthened their ties and dependence on the Chinese market. The sections below will detail French aerospace firms’ deep connections to China. However, it is important to note that French aerospace companies have a history of displacing American rivals internationally, including in China. A WTO compliance panel found the European Union (EU), Germany, France, the United Kingdom, and Spain gave Airbus billions of dollars in subsidies. F203 The WTO panel further found European subsidies caused Airbus to displace Boeing aircraft in China, among other places. F204 This historical case shows that Airbus will displace American aerospace firms even if it goes against allied interests. Were the United States to apply unilateral restrictions on the Chinese market, Airbus and other French companies would displace American incumbents as they have previously. It is therefore important for policymakers to balance PRC aerospace restrictions while not creating an opening for French companies to backfill. Airbus Airbus worked with the Chinese aerospace industrial base across a multitude of capabilities. China is Airbus’s largest sales market. F205 Airbus opened several sprawling facilities in China, including its first A320 FAL outside Europe in Tianjin as described below. Airbus also opened an airplane recycling facility in Chengdu,F206 an A330 finishing facility in Tianjin, it’s first outside Europe, F207 and a FAL for the H135 helicopter in Qingdao. F 208 Beyond these facilities, Airbus significantly invested in the Chinese aerospace technical ecosystem. Airbus opened a research and development center in Suzhou,F209 and  an innovation center in Shenzhen to “[access] a highly advanced digital innovation ecosystem.” F210 While other aerospace companies pulled back from the Chinese market, Airbus tripled down by adding a second FAL with construction beginning in 2023. The resulting facility is a sprawling complex that significantly empowers the Chinese aerospace industrial base. Figure 12, a satellite photo from Vantor, shows the facility’s scale. Figure 12. Satellite Image of Airbus’s Facilities Airbus’ relationship with AVIC has grown beyond joint production and into direct equity ownership. For roughly two decades, Airbus was the single largest international shareholder of AviChina Industry and Technology Company Limited, AVIC’s Hong Kong listed arm, holding a 5 percent stake valued at approximately $140 million. F 211 Airbus’s China CEO, George Xu, concurrently served as a non-executive director of AviChina and a member of its Development and Strategy Committee.F 212 Airbus was therefore not merely a customer and manufacturing partner of AVIC but a financial stakeholder and key decision maker in the listed vehicle of China’s principal military-aviation conglomerate. Airbus divested the entirety of this stake in April 2025, subsequently confirming that it ”does not have any equity investments in AVIC.” F 213 The divestment, however, terminated only the shareholding; Airbus’s operational partnerships with AVIC including joint ventures, wing production, and component supply continue. Beyond equity ownership and industrial investment, Airbus actively encouraged its established Western suppliers to relocate manufacturing capability into China. Airbus’s own China CEO has been explicit on the point, stating that the company encourages its traditional European and American suppliers to come to China, invest, build factories, and cooperate with the Chinese aviation manufacturers, and that Airbus has been actively encouraging its longstanding suppliers to do so.F214 For example, the French aerostructures manufacturer Figeac Aero, which counts Airbus among its principal customers, illustrates the pattern. Its Chinese joint venture, Nanshan Figeac Aero Industry (NFAI), formed with Shandong Nanshan Aluminum, established a Chinese production line for complex monobloc aluminum aerospace parts, investing in advanced machining centers and securing the AS9100 and EN9100 aerospace quality certifications with the technical support of its Chinese partner. F215 In 2024, NFAI was accredited as an approved supplier by AVIC SAC Commercial Aircraft, a subsidiary of AVIC, positioning the French-founded venture directly within AVIC’s supply chain and clearing its path to bid on Chinese aerospace programs. F216  As a result, Airbus directly built French aerospace manufacturing capabilities into China’s aerospace military industrial base. To further entrench itself in the PRC ecosystem, Airbus enmeshed itself directly with the CCP. George Xu (Xu Gang), appointed CEO of Airbus China in January 2018, spent more than two decades working within the Chinese government and Communist Party apparatus before assuming leadership of Airbus’s largest national market. F217 Xu began his career in 1995 at the Tianjin Economic and Technology Development Area Administrative Committee and rose to become the Director of the Investment Promotion Bureau of the Tianjin Free Trade Zone. F218 This was the same government agency that competed to bring the Airbus A320 final assembly line to Tianjin over rival cities including Shanghai, Xi’an, and Zhuhai.F219 In that capacity, Xu directly shaped the project, participating in the site selection and the negotiation of the Airbus joint venture. F220 He held senior government and Airbus-related positions concurrently: from 2011 to 2014 he served simultaneously as Chairman of the Board of the Airbus Tianjin Final Assembly Line and as Vice President of the Tianjin Free Trade Zone Administrative Committee. F221 Subsequently, Airbus settled bribery allegations in China that overlap with that timeframe raising questions about this relationship. F222 From 2014 to 2017, Xu worked full-time in Party organizations, serving as Party Secretary of the Tianjin Municipal Committee of the Communist Youth League and as Standing Committee Member of the Communist Youth League of China Central Committee, alongside a seat on the Standing Committee of the Tianjin Municipal Peoples’s Congress, before moving directly into the CEO role at Airbus China.F 223 Reflecting on the transition, Xu characterized his earlier government work as oriented toward supporting Airbus and ensuring the project succeeded as a ”win-win.”F224 That Xu heads Airbus’s operations in its largest market and came directly from senior Party and municipal government posts underscores the extent to which Airbus’s commercial position in China has been embedded within the Chinese party-state. Finally, Airbus contributed to the Chinese ecosystem beyond aircraft. France and China have cooperated in space for decades, most visibly through the China- France Oceanography Satellite (CFOSAT). F 225 This partnership was launched jointly by the French space agency Centre National d'Études Spatiales (CNES) and the China National Space Administration in 2018 to monitor the ocean surface, winds, and waves, with the resulting data shared bilaterally between French and Chinese mission centers. F226 While the mission is described as civil and scientific, the data exchanges carry recognized dual-use relevance for maritime and naval operations-- a relevance signaled by the French Navy’s hydrographic service (SHOM) being among its partners.F227 That relevance is not abstract. Sea weather remains a decisive constraint on amphibious operations in the Taiwan Strait. F228 Seasonal monsoons and typhoon patterns drive wave heights that dictate naval movements, narrowing any cross- strait amphibious assault by China to two viable windows a year. F229 As a result, understanding and predicting surface and wave patterns present crucial operational information to the PLA as part of any future cross-strait invasion.F230 The DoW assesses that the PLA continues to refine an amphibious invasion among its options to compel unification with Taiwan by force, underscoring the dual-use application of this bilateral exchange of oceanographic data.F231 Airbus Defense and Space is among CNES’s principal industrial partners, building satellites and Earth- observation systems on which French space capability rests, and thus sits at the center of an institutional ecosystem that simultaneously pursues geospatial-data cooperation with China. F232 The connection here is an indication that the same blurring of civil cooperation and strategic exposure running through Airbus’s aviation partnerships also appears in the space domain. Dassault Systèmes International Dassault illustrates the same allied-policy gap at the software layer. The French company’s industrial design and manufacturing tools are widely used to design, simulate, and manage complex aerospace systems. Both Airbus and Dassault were founding members of the France-China business council, launched during President Emmanuel Macron’s January 2018 state visit alongside Chinse partners including COMAC and Huawei.F233 Dassault spun off from the aircraft manufacturer Dassault Aviation in 1981 but is still a part of the broader Dassault group and is among the world’s leading industrial software companies. Its flagship 3DEXPERIENCE platform and constituent applications, including the CATIA design suite, SIMULA simulation tools, and product-lifecycle management software, are used across the aerospace, defense, and advanced manufacturing sectors to design, simulate, and manage the production of complex engineered systems. The company has operated in China since 1986 and works with more than 100 Chinese partners.F234 In 2018, during President Emmanuel Macron’s state visit to China, Dassault signed a strategic cooperation agreement with CASC, a U.S. government listed entity, to deploy its 3DEXPERIENCE platform and strengthen CASC’s digital manufacturing capabilities,F235 which was framed as supporting China’s “Made in China 2025” strategy.F 236 CASC is the principal contractor for China’s space program and, at the same time, a core developer of the PLA’s strategic and tactical missile systems. F237 Dassault subsequently expanded its PRC relationships. Chinese reporting identified CASC-controlled Beijing Shenzhou Aerospace Software Technology Co., Ltd. (“Shenzhou Aerospace”) as the vehicle for integrating Dassault technology into the PRC aerospace industrial base. F 238 Shenzhou Aerospace describes its software as serving aerospace, defense, government, Party, and military customers. It also holds qualifications for military and classified systems. In December 2025, Shenzhou Aerospace and Dassault established Aerospace Xingyuan Digital Intelligence Technology Co., Ltd. to focus on software and information technology services. F239 The 2018 cooperation agreement with CASC was not an abstract memorandum. From the outset it was structured around a joint venture with a specific CASC subsidiary whose business is explicitly military. Chinese reporting on the agreement identified the vehicle for cooperation as Beijing Shenzou Aerospace Software Technology Co., Ltd., a state-owned software enterprise controlled by CASC, which would form a joint venture with Dassault to integrate the 3DEXPERIENCE platform into Chinese aerospace informatization and “further enhance manufacturing capabilities.” F240 CASC’s chief engineer, who also chairs Beijing Shenzou, described the objective plainly: to apply Dassault’s technology in service of ”China Aerospace Manufacturing 2025.” F241 Dassault’s direct partnerships with listed Chinese entities raise questions about its export compliance. Dassault completed a series of United States-based acquisitions to supplement its software offering, including Exa Corporation. F242 Exa Corporation provided software to assist in simulating fluid dynamics and according to former Exa CEO Stephen Remondi, Exa can “solve the most challenging fluids problems faster and more accurately than traditional methods for aerodynamics, aeroacoustics, thermal management and other fluids-related applications.”F243 These statements indicate the software would likely be integrated into Dassault’s offering to CASC. Beyond Exa, Dassault acquired multiple other American software providers including IQMS.244 Dassault’s integration of an American aerodynamics software provider into its offering while simultaneously offering aerodynamics software to listed Chinese users raises questions about Dassault’s export compliance.
