blocks.text: Policy Recommendation 1: Force Defense Contractors to Pick a Side The competition between the United States and the PRC will continue into the foreseeable future. United States and allied companies receiving taxpayer funding should not be able to play both sides of this competition. Allied aerospace companies such as Airbus continue to receive U.S. taxpayer funding while simultaneously investing in both the U.S. and PRC aerospace industrial bases. The United States should not allocate taxpayer dollars to companies that build adversary military capabilities that can be turned against the United States and its allies. Policy Recommendation 2: Restrict Investments in China’s Aerospace Sector, and Expect Allies and Partners to Do the Same The Treasury Department should restrict outbound investment into China’s aerospace sector under its Outbound Investment Security Program, and Congress should codify this prohibition by amending it into the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act of 2025 (COINS Act). The COINS Act framework prohibits investment in certain sectors of the Chinese economy due to their dual- use capabilities. As shown in this investigation, the Chinese aerospace sector deeply intertwines both civil and military capabilities and remains at the heart of China’s Military-Civil Fusion strategy. Simultaneously, the executive branch should pressure allies to act in lockstep and avoid undermining shared security interests. Policy Recommendation 3: The Federal Aviation Administration Should Not Certify Aircraft Manufactured in China Allowing Chinese manufactured aircraft to fly in the United States impacts two key areas of U.S. government policy. First, it impacts the safety of air travel. As described above, China’s aerospace industry remains completely intertwined with its military apparatus. As a result, China withholds critical aircraft safety information on “national security” grounds. For example, when a China Eastern Airlines Boeing aircraft crashed in China, the Chinese government refused to release the report required under China’s international air safety obligations based on “national security and social stability.” F267 Certifying aircraft manufactured in this environment that does not share safety information endangers American passengers. Second, certifying aircraft manufactured in China rewards the lavish subsidies China gave COMAC and AVIC. Policy Recommendation 4: Require Defense and Aerospace Contractors to Disclose Ties to Chinese Military-Designated Entities China’s Military-Civil Fusion strategy deliberately erases the line between its commercial and defense industries, and Western aerospace companies are embedded in both. A single Chinese state-owned enterprise builds wings for Western commercial airliners while simultaneously developing PLA strategic bombers and military transport aircraft. Western firms hold joint ventures, technology transfer agreements, and equity stakes in Chinese enterprises the U.S. government has designated as contributors to China's military modernization and many of those same firms hold contracts with the DoW. While existing law requires contractors to disclose certain supply chain related risks, the DoW has no requirement that contractors disclose their Chinese investments, co-development relationships with PRC military contractors, or other relationships that transfer knowledge to the PRC. Congress should pass the Aerospace Transparency Act (H.R.11047), requiring aerospace contractors doing business with DoW to disclose their relationships with U.S.-designated Chinese military companies, giving the Department the visibility it needs to assess and act on these entanglements. Policy Recommendation 5: Toughen Export Control Licensing and Enforcement for Aerospace Technology Exports to China Aerospace companies transferring controlled technologies to the PRC aerospace industrial base have not been required to disclose the full beneficial ownership of JV partners – even when Chinese military companies hold equity. Significant ITAR violations have been answered with penalties that do not change behavior, much of which the company pays itself to remediate its compliance practices. The State and Commerce Departments should fundamentally reapproach how licensing for aerospace technologies is handled, reducing exports to adversaries generally, requiring full beneficial ownership transparency for all interested parties, denying dual-use exports or exports accessible by Chinese military companies, and enforcing violations with genuinely deterrent penalties. Policy Recommendation 6: Direct the Intelligence Community to Assess the National Security Threat Posed by Commercial Geospatial AI Tools China’s Military-Civil Fusion strategy extends beyond hardware, and Chinese AI firms are now providing adversaries with targeting-grade intelligence derived from commercially available satellite imagery. During the recent conflict involving Iran, Chinese AI firm MizarVision publicly published AI-enhanced analysis of U.S. military positions on open platforms in near real time, and intelligence officials assessed that Iran actively exploited this imagery to target American assets.F 268 AI-enabled geospatial analysis tools that once required state-level F resources are now broadly accessible through commercial software, hosted cloud services, and off-the-shelf platforms. The U.S. currently has no publicly-available comprehensive picture of what these tools can do or how adversaries are using them. Congress should pass the Geospatial Intelligence Transparency and Security Act (H.R.11048), directing the NGA to assess the full landscape of commercial geospatial AI capabilities, identify those presenting the greatest national security concern, and transmit the findings to the Departments of Commerce and State to inform export control rulemaking and international negotiations. Policy Recommendation 7: Subject Acquisition of American Aerospace Companies by French Companies to Heightened Scrutiny and a Presumption of Denial Until They Unwind Ties to China’s Civil-Military Ecosystem As discussed above, French aerospace companies operate under different rules than American firms. French firms maintain much stronger ties to the Chinese aerospace industrial base than American companies. Despite these different rules, French aerospace companies have been able to make acquisitions of U.S. companies as described above with Dassault and Safran’s acquisition of Collins Aerospace’s flight controls unit. 269 When combined with the French blocking statute that prohibits effective oversight, this backdoor allows French companies to buy American capabilities and sell them to Chinese entities designated by the U.S. government for national security-related concerns. Were U.S. regulatory agencies to investigate, the French blocking statute would prohibit effective oversight. For example, during interactions with Airbus, Airbus told the Select Committee that the U.S. Department of Justice could not obtain documents from the company and instead had to rely solely on interviews as part of its criminal investigation. Since French companies also advertise themselves as beyond United States restrictions, CFIUS must apply stricter scrutiny to French acquisitions of key American technology until France unwinds its close integration with the Chinese industrial base. blocks.text: August 14, 2025 Robin Hayes Chief Executive Officer Airbus Americas 2550 Wasser Terrace, Suite 9100 Herndon, VA 20171 Dear Mr. Hayes, The Committee is reviewing U.S. and western aerospace companies’ engagements with the Chinese market. We write to begin a dialogue and request further information regarding Airbus’s ongoing relationship with the Aviation Industry Corporation of China (AVIC). Airbus is a major western defense contractor that has contributed unparalleled capabilities. It appears that Airbus also maintains a longstanding partnership with AVIC, a Chinese state-owned enterprise that directly supports the People’s Liberation Army (PLA)—an entity the United States may one day be forced to confront in a military conflict. The Committee seeks to gain a better understanding of Airbus’s Chinese operations and collaboratively work on strengthening U.S. export control and outbound investment policy. For the past 25 years, the U.S. government and Congress operated under a naïve assumption: robust economic engagement would lead the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) to political liberalization.i In furtherance of this misguided objective, the U.S. government encouraged businesses including aerospace companies such as Airbus to make significant investments in the People’s Republic of China (PRC). The promise of potentially the largest market in the world presented a tremendous opportunity. But the situation has changed. America’s misguided optimism about China turned to clear-eyed confrontation once the U.S. Government finally recognized the threat posed by the CCP. As Congress and the U.S. Government shift their approach towards confronting this existential threat, we expect companies to work with us in good faith to unwind relationships that undermine U.S. national security.ii U.S. export controls help to protect U.S. national security and bolster America’s technological superiority, ensuring that U.S. developed or derived technology does not get used against Americans or to erode our technical edge. In the aerospace domain, there is substantial overlap between commercial and military aerospace technologies, as you know. Advanced commercial technologies—such as integrated flight management systems, engines, modular avionics architectures, cockpit displaysiii, and weather radariv— can be easily repurposed for military use.v The United States pioneered this approach of adapting commercial technology for military systems—repurposing commercial aircraft such as the Boeing 737, 767, and 707 into highly capable military platforms including the P-8 Poseidon, KC-46 Pegasus, and airborne early warning and signals intelligence aircraft.vi However, this was American defense companies supporting the U.S. military. We are concerned about western aerospace companies supporting PRC military capabilities. The PRC aggressively adopted this same approach of developing commercial technology then repurposing it for military purposes. It primarily accomplished this goal by leveraging joint ventures and partnerships with western aerospace companies.vii Many of these joint ventures predate the U.S. Government’s recognition of the CCP threat, but now they should be reevaluated given the national security threat posed by China. Relationships between western aerospace companies and the Chinese industrial base not only transferred technology but also taught PRC firms the critical design, manufacturing, and certification know-how needed to develop China’s indigenous aircraft.viii By bypassing early phases of aerospace development, these partnerships helped China rapidly modernize the People’s Liberation Army Air Force (PLAAF), ix largely through one key firm: AVIC. AVIC is not a benign commercial partner. It produces essentially all of China’s domestic fixed-wing military aircraft, UAVs, and helicopters, as well as a wide range of civilian aircraft and other aviation and nonaviation products and services.x Unlike its western counterparts, AVIC’s primary duty is not to shareholders, but to the PRC Party-state and its defense goals, particularly through Beijing’s strategy of military-civil fusion [ ].xi In recognition of this role, the U.S. Treasury Department designated AVIC a Non-SDN Chinese Military- Industrial Complex Company in 2021.xii The Committee has concerns that Airbus’s work with AVIC enables PLAAF aircraft development through AVIC. Airbus’s relationship with the PRC dates back several decades. Airbus’s China CEO Xu Gang—himself a former Chinese Communist Party member who holds a degree from an entity listed universityxiii—described Airbus as “a member of the Chinese aviation industry family.”xiv Airbus’s “long-term strategic partnership” with AVIC has been a key avenue for supporting PRC aviation goals. Airbus’s AVIC partnership involves sharing core Airbus technologies, such as polymer nanocomposites with aeronautic applications,xv and wing technology.xvi This partnership includes joint ventures, supply relationships, and production of key wing technology.xvii Notably, AVIC subsidiary Xi’an Aircraft Industry Group Co. (XAC) manufactures A320 wings assembled at Airbus’s Tianjin facility,xviii however, XAC also develops and produces AVIC’s H-20 bomber aircraft.xix For the A350, the Airbus-AVIC joint venture involved PRC companies from the early stages and allowed Chinese companies to participate in research and development, design, as well as manufacturing.xx These years of development culminated in Tianjin being the only city outside Europe that can deliver both single-aisle and widebody Airbus aircraft.xxi Some relationships, such as the one with XAC, date back to 2009, before America fully appreciated the CCP threat. However, with the U.S. pivot on the CCP, we expect Airbus to pivot with us and unwind these relationships that contribute to the PRC’s aviation industrial base. Airbus also appears to enable China’s pursuit of advanced capabilities across multiple domains. It supports China’s satellite program through its joint venture with the Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing Spot Image Co. Ltd., which has supplied satellite imagery to Chinese government agencies for over two decades. xxiii xxii Furthermore, Airbus’s China Innovation Center, launched in 2018, focuses on areas with direct military relevance such as 5G connectivity and the Beidou satellite navigation system, a core pillar of the CCP’s military-civil fusion strategy. While Airbus supports the civilian section of these technologies, we are worried they could be used by the PRC military. For example, the Beidou satellite system mirrors the U.S. Global Positioning System (GPS).xxiv GPS represents a core technology for U.S. military aircraft, vessels, vehicles, and personnel.xxv Developing a Chinese analog enables the PLA to integrate this critical system into its military aircraft, vessels, and other vehicles. Announcements by Airbus helicopters illustrate our concerns. First, Airbus Helicopter’s sale of models with an available military variant risks giving China a helicopter that it could easily repurpose for its military. Second, Airbus Helicopters’ joint development of a heavy-lift helicopter transfers critical development know-how that could be applied to military helicopters. In 2022, Airbus Helicopters signed a USD $700 million contract with GDAT, a state-owned Chinese helicopter leasing company, for H160 helicopters. xxvii xxvi Airbus also sold a military variant of the same platform—the H160M “Guépard”— to the French Ministry of Armed Forces for its Light Joint Helicopter Program, with deliveries beginning in 2027. Selling the H160 to a state-owned Chinese company gives it a platform that could be reconfigured for military use. In the west, we operate with clear delineations between private enterprises and the government so that helicopters sold to a private company are unlikely to end up in military service. China lacks these boundaries. The helicopters that Airbus sold to GDAT can conscripted by the PRC party- state and reconfigured for military operations, with the H160M offering a model to follow. We are most concerned about Airbus’ joint development of the Z-15 helicopter with the Harbin Aircraft Industry Group,xxviii xxxii because the same company develops military helicopters for the Chinese military.xxix We understand that this development relationship dates back to 2006, before we realized the threat posed by the PRC, but it illustrates our worry. Through this arrangement, Airbus transfers key know-how and enables the People’s Liberation Army to further advance its helicopter capabilities. Around the time of its announcement, in 2006, China Dailyxxx, a state-owned newspaperxxxi, published the following mockup of the Z-15: practices through this collaboration. AVIC can then take those same technologies and apply them to the design, production, and maintenance of military aircraft. In totality, this collaboration creates a dual-use pathway allowing AVIC to enhance the design and performance of PLAAF platforms using the technological know-how developed with Airbus on COMAC. The PRC government recognizes this fact and enables AVIC’s technological development by giving it an outsized influence on COMAC operations. We hope this letter initiates a dialogue that leads to Airbus unwinding or substantially curtailing its PRC operations. In furtherance of these goals, we request production of documents in the following categories as soon as possible but no later than August 28, 2025:xxxviii

Technical specifications of products and services developed under these partnerships, including their associated control status and number under U.S. export control regulations, even if those items are not subject to the Export Administration Regulations.

A complete list in native Microsoft Excel of Airbus’s (including all predecessor companies) subsidiaries, joint ventures, partnerships, subcontracts, affiliates, intermediaries, licensees in the PRC, and any entities receiving technology, services, and training in the PRC, including but not limited to AVIC or any of its known subsidiaries (collectively “Ventures in the PRC”).
A complete list in native Microsoft Excel of all technology transferred to AVIC, its subsidiaries, intermediaries, affiliates, and agents (including the PRC government).

All due diligence materials and internal compliance assessments relating to any joint venture or partner in China, including but not limited to those addressing potential military end-use or end-users or addressing transfers of Technical Data or Technology under U.S. export control regulations.

Communications with any U.S. government agency (e.g., Departments of State, Commerce, or Defense) regarding ventures in the PRC as defined in Number 2 above (Note: this is a continuing request, meaning that subsequent disclosures made after this letter's date should be considered as included)

All communications from Airbus’s trade compliance (or its equivalent) team about any and all potential or actual export control violations related to AVIC and Ventures in the PRC as defined in Number 2 above.
All communications from Airbus’s Empowered Official(s) mentioning, discussing, raising, or communicating in any way about any and all issues both potential and actual related to the PRC.

Copies of all export licenses mentioning or involving AVIC, its subsidiaries, intermediaries, affiliates, and agents (including the PRC government) for all Ventures in the PRC as defined in Number 2 above.
A complete list in native Microsoft Excel of all academic or research relationships, Airbus maintains with PRC-based universities, innovation hubs, or research centers.
A complete list of all CCP members who work for Airbus, its subsidiaries, intermediaries, affiliates, and agents.

An accounting under International Financial Reporting Standards produced in native Microsoft Excel of the profit and losses from the PRC-based joint ventures, as well as the value of all capital contributed to AVIC, including through its subsidiaries, joint ventures, partnerships, subcontracts, affiliates, intermediaries, licensees, or any other entity related to AVIC.
An accounting under International Financial Reporting Standards produced in native Microsoft Excel of all profit and losses associated with the Ventures in the PRC as defined in Number 2 above.

Congress finds the following: (1) The People’s Republic of China pursues a national strategy of military-civil fusion, under which the Chinese Communist Party seeks to ac- quire and direct advanced technology, expertise, and industrial capability developed by nominally civilian and commercial entities toward the modernization of the People’s Liberation Army. (2) Under this strategy, the distinction between China’s civilian and military industrial bases is de- liberately eroded, such that commercial partnerships, technology transfers, and investments involving Chi- nese enterprises may contribute, directly or indi- rectly, to the development of military capabilities of the People’s Republic of China. (3) Aerospace, aviation, and space technologies are among the priority sectors of the military mod- ernization of the People’s Republic of China and among the priority sectors of its national industrial strategy. (4) The United States Government has formally identified numerous Chinese enterprises as contribu- tors to China’s defense-industrial base or military modernization through multiple designation regimes, including the list of Chinese military companies maintained by the Secretary of Defense pursuant to section 1260H of the National Defense Authoriza- tion Act for Fiscal Year 2021 (10 U.S.C. 113 note), the Non-SDN Chinese Military-Industrial Complex Companies List maintained by the Secretary of the Treasury, the Entity List set forth in Supplement No. 4 to part 744 of the Export Administration Regulations , and the Military End User List set forth in Supplement No. 7 to part 744 of the Export Administration Regulations. (5) These designations reflect a determination by the United States Government that the identified entities present a national security concern by virtue of their role in, or support for, military moderniza- tion of the People’s Republic of China. (6) Documented cases demonstrate that a sin- gle Chinese state-owned enterprise may simulta- neously serve as a supplier or manufacturing partner to Western commercial aerospace programs and as a principal developer of military aircraft for the Peo- ple’s Liberation Army, including strategic bombers and military transport aircraft, such that commer- cial cooperation with that enterprise is not readily separable form its military production. (7) Advance Western industrial design, simula- tion, and manufacturing software has been use din the development of fielded combat aircraft of the People’s Liberation Army, demonstrating that com- mercially available engineering tools can materially contribute to the design and production of foreign military systems. (8) Western firms have entered into joint ven- tures, technology-transfer agreements, co-production agreements, and equity investments with Chinese en- terprises that the United States Government has designated as contributors to China’s military mod- ernization, or with subsidiaries of such enterprises, including enterprises engaged in the development of military aircraft, missiles, and space systems. (9) In certain of these cases, the firm engaged in such a relationship holds, directly or through a parent company or an entity under common control, contracts, subcontracts, grants, or other agreements with the Department of Defense. (10) There is at present no comprehensive re- quirement that entities holding aerospace-related contracts, subcontracts, grants, or other agreements with the Department of Defense disclose to the De- partment their relationships, or the relationships of their corporate affiliates, with entities designated by the United States Government as contributors to China’s military modernization. (11) As a result, the Department of Defense lacks visibility into supply chain, security and capa- bility transfer risks arising from the relationships that its contractors, or the corporate affiliates of its contractors, maintain with such designated entities. (12) Such visibility is necessary for the Depart- ment of Defense to assess and, where warranted, mitigate risks to the integrity of the defense aero- space supply chain and to the security of Depart- ment of Defense programs. (13) The United States retains the authority to establish, as a condition of eligibility for contract, subcontracts, grants, and other agreements with the Department of Defense, requirements that contrac- tors disclose information material to the national se- curity interests of the United States. (14) Requiring disclosure of relationships with designated entities, while reserving to the Depart- ment of Defense the assessment of such relation- ships and any determination regarding their con- sequences, is a measured and appropriately limited means of clsing the visibility gap described in this section.

(d) DEFINITIONS.—In this section: (1) The term ‘‘controlled technology’’ means technology— (A) described in or otherwise classified under the Commerce Control List set forth in Supplement No. 1 to part 774 of the Export Administration Regulations; or (B) subject to the Export Administration Regulations but not described in or otherwise classified under the Commerce Control List. designated as EAR99. (2) The term ‘‘covered contractor’’ means a contractor performing a covered contract on the date of the enactment of this Act. (3) The term ‘‘covered contract’’ means a con- tract, grant, or other transaction agreement offered by the Department of Defense for the design, devel- opment, production, sustainment, or supply of cov- ered aerospace technology. (4) The term ‘‘covered aerospace technology’’ means software, intellectual property, or technology used in the design, development, simulation, produc- tion, or sustainment of aircraft, spacecraft, launch vehicles, propulsion systems, avionics, or related sys- tems and subsystems intended for use by the De- partment of Defense. (6) The term ‘‘covered entity’’ means— (A) any entity on— (i) the list of Chinese military compa- nies maintained by the Secretary of De- fense pursuant to section 1260H of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021 (10 U.S.C. 113 note); (ii) the Non-SDN Chinese Military-In- dustrial Complex Companies List main- tained by the Secretary of the Treasury; (iii) the Entity List set forth in Sup- plement No. 4 to part 744 of the Export Administration Regulations; or (iv) the Military End User List set forth in Supplement No. 7 to part 744 of the Export Administration Regulations; or (B) any entity that is majority-owned by an entity described in subparagraph (A).
